title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
abstract: arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depend

translated_title: 数绷带：论如何衡量AI节省的时间
translated_abstract: arXiv:2610.35942v1 公告类型：新论文 摘要：我探讨了AI辅助“节省时间”究竟意味着什么。我对比了两种观点：一种是“秒表观点”，即节省的时间就是时钟所记录的时间；另一种是“账本观点”，即节省的时间是一种反事实量，必须结合工作中被放过去的错误来解读。我论证支持后者。论证分为四个部分。我定义了一组不依赖具体模型的量——节省的时间和超额逃逸缺陷数，以及由它们构造出的一个决策数字：盈亏平衡缺陷成本。我给出了一个关于检查工作的基线模型，在该模型中，只要模型还没有好到可以不检查的程度，一个校准良好的工作者的逃逸缺陷率就不依赖于模型的好坏；检查时间随模型错误率的对数增长；而过度信任虽然在时钟上买来了几分钟，却要以总时间上更大的代价为成本。我说明了随机化研究能识别什么、不能识别什么，并从公开数据复现了METR的开发者研究：同样的246个问题既支持19%也支持24%的速度下降，取决于……（原文摘要在此处被截断）
tldr: 论文主张应以结合逃逸缺陷的“账本观点”而非单纯计时的“秒表观点”来衡量AI节省的时间，定义了节省时间、超额逃逸缺陷和盈亏平衡缺陷成本等量，证明只要仍需人工检查，校准良好的工作者逃逸缺陷率与模型质量无关，并从公开数据复现METR开发者研究，显示同一数据可支持19%或24%的速度下降。
en_tdlr: The paper argues that AI time savings should be measured via a counterfactual "ledger view" read alongside escaped defects rather than a stopwatch view, defining time saved, excess escaped defects, and a break-even defect cost, showing that calibrated workers' escaped-defect rates are independent of model quality until checking becomes unnecessary, and replicating METR's developer study from public data, where the same 246 issues support either a 19% or a 24% slowdown.
